description:
perf(evm): front the EVM call pools with a per-thread free list (#12905)

* perf(evm): front the EVM call pools with a per-thread free list

The four pools the call machinery rents from - EVM stacks, VmState frames,
ExecutionEnvironment and the StackAccessTracker state - were each a single
ConcurrentQueue shared process-wide, so every frame of every thread contended
on one segment head. Profiling eth_call at 100rps put ~1.8% of the ARM subtree
in SpinWait.SpinOnce inside TryDequeue, 4.4x the x64 cost (124,071 vs 28,190
sampled OwnTime units): a contended CAS is far more expensive under arm64 LL/SC
and its weak memory model than under x86 TSO.

Frames rent and return in LIFO order on one thread, so EvmObjectPool serves
them from a per-thread free list with no atomics at all, keeping the shared
queue for overflow from deep frames and cross-thread imbalance. The stack pool
retains 8 per thread since its items are ~32KB and pinned; the shared tier keeps
the existing MaxStacksPooled bound.

The guest keeps ZkEvmQueue, so its single-threaded path is unchanged.

* perf(evm): make the stack pool a process-wide singleton, correct its bound

Review of the previous commit surfaced two issues.

StackPool lived in VmState's statics, so the number of stack pools
tracked the number of closed VmState<> types even though a stack carries no
gas-policy state. A second IGasPolicy would therefore have created a second
EvmObjectPool, and since the per-thread free list is static per
closed generic type the two would have shared it - tripping the debug assertion
in Debug and double-provisioning the pinned budget in Release. Hoisting the
instance to StackPool.Shared makes the invariant structural and drops the
per-closed-type duplication.

The comment also claimed retention "stays bounded by MaxStacksPooled as before",
which is only true of the shared tier. Corrected to state the real ceiling:
MaxStacksPooled plus LocalStacksPooled per thread that has run an EVM frame,
which matters because RegisterRpcModules raises the thread-pool minimum by
ProcessorCount and those threads are never retired.

* perf(evm): address review on the pooling change

- annotate both TryDequeue overloads with [MaybeNullWhen(false)], matching
  ConcurrentQueue. Without it the compiler treats the out param as non-null
  after a false return, which quietly undermines the repo rule of trusting null
  annotations instead of adding redundant checks.
- validate the constructor's capacities. A negative localCapacity previously
  surfaced as an exception from `new T[]` inside Enqueue, on whichever thread
  happened to return an item first, far from the construction site.
- hoist the Interlocked.Increment out of the Debug.Assert condition. It was only
  correct because the whole block sits inside #if DEBUG; anyone removing that
  wrapper - reasonable, since Debug.Assert is already [Conditional("DEBUG")] -
  would have turned the guard into Assert(1 == 1).
- give StackPool a private constructor now that Shared exists, so the
  single-instance invariant EvmObjectPool relies on is structural rather than a
  debug-only assertion. A second instance would trade stacks with Shared and
  silently inherit whichever capacity allocated a thread's array first.
- correct the _sharedCount remark: a warm thread never reaches the shared queue
  at all, so the zero-check helps a thread whose local free list is empty.
- make the churn test assert on steady-state allocations instead of a cumulative
  budget. Round 0 is entitled to the whole working set against an empty pool, so
  the old `< 2 * threads * itemsPerThread` bound left only ~0.2% headroom for
  TryDequeueShared losing the publish race - a race rate, not the invariant.

* perf(evm): give the tracker pool one local slot, trim the comments

StackAccessTracker is rented at RentTopLevel, once per top-level execution rather than per frame, and
nesting is handled inside one tracker by TakeSnapshot/Restore. A thread therefore has one live at a
time, so 16 local slots could never be used while each retained state keeps its journal sets and hash
sets at the high-water capacity of whatever transaction last used them - the largest unbounded
retention in this PR. One slot keeps the whole win: the state returns to the local slot and the next
execution rents it straight back, no atomics.

Also trim the comments on the pooling change, which had grown to a third of the added lines. The
arm64 CAS rationale, the reads-high-never-low invariant behind the shared-count fast path, the
one-instance-per-type constraint and the pinned-ceiling arithmetic stay; the restatements of the
code they sit above do not.

* test(evm): count steady-state pool allocations per thread

The warm-up snapshot was taken by whichever thread reached round 1 first, so a lagging thread still in
round 0 had its allocations billed to the steady state - roughly two workers' worth against a tolerance
of 128. Counting each thread's own post-warm-up allocations makes the figure exact.

A Barrier would also close it, but Parallel.For is free to run 8 iterations on fewer than 8 threads, so
a barrier of 8 participants inside its body risks never being satisfied.

* test(evm): stop asserting a scheduling-dependent allocation rate

Reproducing the reported failure with 14 spinning processes on a 16-thread box showed the previous
commit's per-thread accounting was not enough: the churn test still failed 2 of 5 loaded runs at 185
and 319 allocations. The warm-up boundary was never the cause. Under CPU starvation a worker
legitimately finds its local list empty and the shared tier transiently drained, because the other
seven hold the whole 512-item working set while descheduled, so it allocates. That rate tracks
scheduling, not pool correctness, and no boundary fixes it.

Assert what the concurrent test can actually establish - no instance handed to two renters, nothing
lost, and recycling happening at all - with a bound loose enough to be scheduling-independent: a pool
that stopped recycling would allocate 256,000 instances against a limit of 2,048. Per-instance reuse
stays pinned by the single-threaded tests.

Workers also move from Parallel.For to dedicated threads, which is orthogonal but was the other half
of the report: Parallel.For may run the eight iterations on fewer threads, and the duplicate check
would then pass without ever renting concurrently. Exceptions are carried out explicitly, since a
thread body would otherwise swallow them and a silent worker would look like a pass.

Loaded: 8 of 8 passing. Unloaded: pool suite 3x green, Nethermind.Evm.Test 5039 total, 0 failed.

* fix(evm): enforce one pool per item type outside DEBUG

The per-thread free list is static per closed generic type, so two EvmObjectPool over one T share it:
each would hand out the other's items - two live renters of one VmState or one 32.9 KB pinned stack -
and the second would silently inherit whichever localCapacity sized the thread's array first, since the
bound reads local.Length. The type's remarks nominate the Debug.Assert as the guard against exactly
this, but Debug.Assert is erased from Release and AGENTS.md prescribes dotnet test -c release, so it was
compiled into neither the shipped node nor CI.

Throw instead. Every pool is a static field initialiser, so a violation now fails at type
initialisation rather than corrupting frames under concurrency, and the cost is one interlocked
increment per pool - four times in a process lifetime, nothing on the hot path.

Nothing violates it today: four pools over four distinct types. The counter is deliberately never
decremented, so a test wanting a second pool needs a distinct T, as the new test does.
product_or_resource: perf(evm): front the EVM call pools with a per-thread free list (#12905)

description:
<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>Add private eth_call corpus mode to the RPC benchmark workflow (#12704)

* rpcbench: small robustness fixes for node lifecycle scripts

- validate eth_blockNumber results as hex before arithmetic in wait_for_rpc
- run db_fingerprint in a subshell in stop-node.sh so a fingerprint failure
  cannot abort teardown (it die()s internally)
- docker rm -fv so anonymous volumes from stale containers are reaped too

* rpcbench: add private eth_call corpus mode with cross-client parity

Adds an opt-in mode (tool_config.eth_call_corpus) to jsonbench and
jsonbench-sweep that makes it possible to benchmark eth_call workloads whose
contents must not appear in Action logs or artifacts (e.g. privately shared
call sets). Corpus files live only on the benchmark runner; jobs publish
sanitized aggregate summaries and counts-only parity reports.

- run-rpc-sweep.sh discovers every eth-call-corpus*.jsonl.gz on the runner as
  its own scenario: latency cells per rps plus a full-corpus replay per client,
  with the first client as the response-parity baseline. Clients (ctype@image),
  rps_list, and duration are free-form. Corpus cells raise the uniform
  RPC_GAS_CAP to 1e12 so explicit multi-billion gas fields are not clamped.
- corpus_parity.py replays the corpus and compares result bytes against the
  baseline; calls both clients reject count as agreement; reports carry
  counters, client labels, and divergent record indexes (positions only).
- corpus_results.py sanitizes k6 summaries to a fixed numeric schema and
  stages only validated aggregate files for the artifact upload.
- prepare-eth-call-corpus.py converts JSONL(.gz) corpora into the JSON-array
  fixture json-bench consumes (its JSONL reader caps lines at ~64 KiB).
- Raw tool output stays in VM scratch; node logs are scanned with the usual
  gates but print counts only; deep-check/HTML are disabled in corpus mode.
- Behavioral unit tests for both modules and the converter; README section
  documenting the privacy contract and dispatch recipes; friendlier
  tool_config input docs; sweep summary gains avg/median columns.

* rpcbench: corpus_glob tool_config filter to select specific corpus files

* rpcbench: address review findings on the corpus mode

- corpus_parity: classify non-200 responses carrying a JSON-RPC error envelope
  as rpc_error instead of transport_failure (status handling is not uniform
  across clients/proxies); record head+chain identity in the baseline state and
  fail compare() with a distinct 'identity mismatch' error so a snapshot at a
  different block is not reported as client divergence; new 'validate'
  subcommand (record count only).
- run-rpc-sweep.sh: validate every discovered corpus before the first node
  starts, turning fixture problems into seconds-long failures.
- corpus_results: treat absent checks/http_req_failed like dropped_iterations
  (k6 omits them when nothing triggered them) instead of failing the cell.
- workflow: single-node jsonbench corpus runs get the same 1e12 RPC_GAS_CAP as
  sweep cells, so both dispatch modes agree.

* rpcbench: reject colliding corpus scenario labels up front

corpus_label sanitizes the filename, so two distinct corpora can collapse onto the
same label and then share a parity baseline and cell directory: the second baseline
overwrites the first, and every later client diffs against the wrong one. It fails
safe - a count mismatch rather than false agreement - but only deep into the sweep,
with a message that points at nothing real.

The labels are already computed for the scenario line, so detecting a duplicate
there costs nothing and turns a confusing mid-sweep failure into an up-front one.

* rpcbench: make the two corpus readers agree, and gate the single-node path

corpus_parity and prepare-eth-call-corpus disagreed on what a legal corpus is, so a
free-form corpus_glob could clear validation in seconds and then die inside the first
latency cell: the converter hard-requires a .jsonl/.jsonl.gz suffix and rejects NaN
and friends via parse_constant, while load_corpus accepted any filename and plain
json.loads. Both checks now live in load_corpus, which is the gate, and a malformed
constant reports a line number rather than escaping as a traceback (JSONDecodeError
is itself a ValueError, so the handler catches both).

The record ceiling also only existed on the sweep path, because it lives in
load_corpus and single-node jsonbench never called it - a corpus the sweep rejects in
seconds was instead converted into a multi-GB fixture and handed to k6. That path now
runs the same validate step next to its existing file-exists check.

Finally, the privacy section covered call contents but not filenames, which become
the public scenario label via corpus_label - the one thing a third party handing over
a corpus would not expect. Says so now, along with the two limits that bite in
practice: the 10k record cap, and a k6 fixture that scales with record count.

* rpcbench: size corpus cells by request count instead of wall time

A corpus cell could only be described as 'this rate for this long', so covering a large
capture meant computing the duration by hand per rate, and the request count drifted
whenever either input changed. corpus_requests states the count directly; corpus_passes
states it as a multiple of the corpus's own record count, reusing the count that the
up-front validate step already prints. Either derives the cell length as
ceil(count / rps), which is exact because k6's constant-arrival-rate executor holds the
rate - the rate asked for is still the rate applied, only the length is computed.

Neither key set leaves cells on JB_DURATION exactly as before.

* rpcbench: make the corpus record cap an opt-in override

MAX_CORPUS_RECORDS was a hard 10k wall, so a larger capture could not be replayed at
all even on a runner with the memory for it. It stays 10k by default - the replay holds
every record's params in memory, so the cost should not be discovered mid-sweep - but is
now raised deliberately via max_corpus_records / RPC_BENCH_MAX_CORPUS_RECORDS.

* rpcbench: add a per-record latency matrix for corpus replays

The k6 cells cannot say which corpus record a latency belongs to: corpus mode collapses
every record into one named call, so all requests carry identical tags, and the
generator samples with replacement while recording only a sequential row id. Aggregate
percentiles are all that path can produce.

The replay path already walks the corpus in order and knows each record's index, so a
timings subcommand there gets the attribution for free: it replays the corpus --passes
times, paces submissions to --rps, and writes one row per record with one column per
pass. Every record is hit exactly --passes times rather than a random number of times,
which is what makes the rows comparable across clients and across branches.

Output is record indexes and milliseconds only, so it publishes under the same boundary
as the parity reports, and the achieved rate is printed so a run that could not sustain
--rps is visible instead of quietly slower.

* rpcbench: run the per-record timing matrix from a sweep

The timings replay only existed as a manual command, so it could not be used against a
corpus living on the runner. It now runs per client inside a corpus sweep, writing
timings.csv alongside that client's parity report, gated on timings_passes.

An empty rps_list now runs no k6 cells. That combination is the only way to drive a
large corpus at a high rate: the k6 path materializes one full payload per request into
its CSV, so 100k requests of ~300KB records is tens of GB before the node is even
touched, while the replay holds one corpus in memory and streams requests at the target
rate.

* rpcbench: let an explicitly empty rps_list mean no k6 cells

The sweep script skips its k6 cells when RPS_LIST is empty, but the workflow made that
unreachable: '// empty' cannot distinguish an absent key from one set to "", so an
explicit empty value was overwritten with the 100/250/500 default. A corpus run asking
for parity and timings only therefore got three k6 cells per client instead of none -
on a large corpus that is the JSON fixture plus tens of GB of generated CSV, exactly
what the request was avoiding.

Keyed on has("rps_list") now: absent means default, empty means no cells.

* rpcbench: stop the sweep default clobbering an explicit empty rps_list

Same defect as the workflow layer, one level down: RPS_LIST used ${VAR:-default}, which
substitutes on empty as well as unset, so an explicitly empty value asking for no k6
cells was replaced by 100/250/500. Fixing only the workflow left the script overriding
it right back. ${VAR-default} substitutes on unset alone, which is the intent.

* rpcbench: report progress during long corpus replays

A 50k-record replay is a single sequential loop that printed only on entry and exit, so
an operator watching the job saw one line and then ~17 minutes of nothing, with no way
to tell a slow node from a hung one. Baseline and compare now emit a count, rate and ETA
every 2000 records, and load_corpus reports its own duration when decompressing and
parsing takes more than a few seconds - on a multi-GB corpus that alone is minutes.

* rpcbench: replay the parity corpus concurrently

The replay issued one request at a time, so wall clock was records x per-call latency and
the node sat ~99% idle: 50k heavy eth_calls took ~17 minutes per client to do a few
seconds of work, and dominated a corpus sweep. At 497 records it cost 10 seconds and
never warranted attention.

eth_call is read-only and deterministic against a parked head, so replaying concurrently
cannot change what any record returns - only how fast the set is collected - and results
are stored by index, so completion order does not matter. Baseline and compare now share
one indexed thread-pool replay, 16 in flight by default
(RPC_BENCH_PARITY_CONCURRENCY). Measured 10x on a 20ms-per-call node with byte-identical
results, taking 50k records from ~17 min to ~2 min per client.

* rpcbench: re-run non-clean parity records serially before reporting them

Replaying concurrently introduces a failure mode the serial loop could not have: a node
under load can drop or truncate a response, and that is indistinguishable from a real
divergence in the report. A correctness gate that invents defects under load is worse
than a slow one.

Two serial re-runs now stand between the concurrent replay and the report. Any record
whose outcome was transport_failure or invalid_response is re-run unloaded, and in
compare any record that disagrees with the baseline at all is re-verified the same way -
cheap, because disagreements are rare. A record that only fails while requests overlap
is a load artifact; one that reproduces unloaded is a defect. rpc_error is deliberately
not retried: a captured corpus legitimately contains calls that fail at the pinned head.

Both directions are covered by tests: a node failing only while overlapping still
reports 30/30 matched and clean, while a client returning reproducibly wrong results for
two records is still caught with exactly those indexes.

* rpcbench: publish the per-record timing matrix

stage() copies an allowlist of aggregate files, and timings.csv was never added to it
when the timing matrix was wired into the sweep - so a completed run produced the matrix
on the runner and then threw it away at upload. It is staged now, behind a validator
that admits only a record_index column, pass_N_ms columns, and numeric or empty cells,
so the same boundary that keeps call contents out of the parity reports applies here.

* rpcbench: record per-record outcome in the timing matrix

The matrix held durations only, with success counts printed once to stdout and stored
nowhere. Anything reading timings.csv therefore could not tell a fast answer from a fast
failure - and a node shedding load posts excellent percentiles, because rejected calls
return early and pull every percentile down. A 500 rps run where a quarter of the calls
were rejected read as a decisive win.

Each pass now writes a status beside its duration, JSON-RPC error codes are kept (an
integer code is protocol metadata, not call content, and is what separates 'this call
reverts' from 'the node is rejecting work'), and a run with any non-ok outcome prints an
explicit warning that its percentiles are not comparable. The staging validator accepts
the status column against a fixed vocabulary plus optional code, so content still cannot
ride out in it.

* rpcbench: optionally characterise each parity divergence

A parity report says how many records diverged and which, never how. Diagnosing a
cross-client disagreement then means re-running the calls by hand, and the divergence
indexes are capped at 200 so a larger disagreement cannot even be enumerated.

The cap is now configurable, and parity_diffs opts in to a word-by-word characterisation
of every content mismatch: response lengths, which 32-byte words differ, their values,
and the numeric delta between them - a fee- or balance-shaped difference shows up as a
clean integer gap. It is derived from response bytes, so it stays off unless asked for,
and it records a bounded structural summary rather than whole responses.

* rpcbench: actually write the divergence characterisations

The characterisations were computed and appended, and then never written: the patch that
added the output block failed partway and only its CLI half was repaired, so a run with
parity_diffs enabled produced the analysis in memory and dropped it. Also wires the
divergence-index cap as a workflow input - it was made configurable but had no input, so
it silently stayed at 200 and could not enumerate a larger disagreement.

Covered end to end: a client short by exactly gas*gasPrice on two records now yields a
diffs file naming those records and reporting the delta.

* rpcbench: bound staged divergences by the record count, not the runtime cap

Staging runs in a separate process from the replay, so an env-tuned
RPC_BENCH_MAX_DIVERGENCE_INDEXES is invisible to the validator: it fell back to the 200
default and rejected a report that had legitimately enumerated 555. The whole run was
discarded at upload after the analysis had already been produced.

A report cannot have more divergences than records, which is the real invariant and one
that holds regardless of how the producer was configured.

* rpcbench: address review — corpus-mode parse, diffs privacy, empty rps_list

High: corpus mode was parsed three ways. A present-but-non-Boolean eth_call_corpus (the
string "true") read as false in resolve while the run steps' tostring read it as true,
so the private corpus was processed with log redaction, restricted staging and the
raised gas cap all disabled. resolve now rejects a non-Boolean and is the single source
of truth; the run steps consume that value instead of reparsing.

High: parity-diffs.json was staged with no validation while carrying complete baseline
and candidate 32-byte response words, contradicting the counts-only boundary the corpus
mode rests on. The words are gone - a signed decimal delta identifies a fee- or
balance-shaped divergence without carrying the operands - and an exact-schema validator
now rejects any field outside {index, lengths, all-zero flags, word position, delta},
covering re-added operands, smuggled strings and hex-shaped deltas.

High: an empty rps_list is documented as "no k6 cells", but zero summaries then hit the
"every client failed to start" exit before the parity table rendered, so every
parity/timings-only run reported failure after doing its work. That case is now distinct
from a genuinely failed sweep.

Medium: node identity is pinned by head block hash, not height+chain id, so a same-height
reorg or mislabelled snapshot is reported as a fixture problem rather than as client
divergence; timings.meta.json records block identity, passes, target/achieved rps and
concurrency so a matrix cannot be silently compared against one taken under different
settings; and the free-form request/pass/rate knobs are validated as positive integers
before any node starts, instead of a value like "250k" collapsing to an empty duration
and silently using the workload default.

Low: truncated-gzip and invalid-UTF-8 corpora raised EOFError/zlib.error/UnicodeError,
which are not OSError and escaped as tracebacks printing corpus bytes; they are
content-free CorpusParityErrors now. total_differing_words reported the capped preview
length rather than the real count.

Tests: same-height/different-hash, corrupt-corpus leak, over-cap word count, and
sentinel-leak staging for the diffs schema.

* rpcbench: run a fixed corpus A/B and comment when a PR is labelled 'performance is good'

Comparing a PR's eth_call performance meant dispatching the workflow by hand and
choosing a corpus, rate and baseline each time, so results were rarely comparable
between PRs.

The label now runs a hard-coded configuration - the 497-record corpus, 100 rps for 120s,
the PR build against nethermind:master as the parity baseline - and posts a comment with
per-metric deltas and the parity verdict. The configuration is fixed in resolve rather
than read from an input precisely so it cannot drift per PR.

The comment is rendered from the staged tree rather than the raw output directory, so
the aggregate-only validator gates everything that reaches a public comment. It also
states the two things needed to read it: a parity divergence is a correctness regression
whatever the latency says, and deltas under about 2.5% are noise on this corpus.

* rpcbench: reuse a connection per replay worker; refresh the timings docs

urllib opened and tore down a TCP connection for every request, folding connect cost into
each measurement and churning ephemeral ports across a 100k-request replay. Each worker
thread now keeps one connection, retrying once because a pooled connection closed by the
peer is indistinguishable from a real failure on first use, and dropping the connection
when an over-long body would leave unread bytes on the socket. Verified: 50 sequential
requests now open one connection instead of 50, with response classification unchanged.

The README example was not executable (no python3 prefix, unwrapped arguments) and still
showed the pre-status CSV shape. It now documents the per-pass status column and why it
exists - a rejected call returns early, so without it a node shedding load reads as a
fast one - the timings.meta.json sidecar, and that matrices are only comparable when
their metadata matches. Also reconciled the fixed-cap text with max_corpus_records.

* rpcbench: sample node resource use alongside the latency numbers

Latency says how long a call took; it cannot say whether a client is slower because it
does more work, because it waits on IO, or because it leaves the machine idle. Nothing in
the harness recorded that, so a cross-client gap could not be attributed.

Samples the benchmarked container's cgroup v2 counters for the duration of a cell and
emits CPU seconds and average/peak cores, average and peak memory, block IO, CPU
throttling, and PSI stall totals for cpu/io/memory - plus CPU-ms and IO-bytes per
request, which is what makes two clients directly comparable. Read from the host cgroup
rather than inside the container, since the three client images differ in what tooling
they carry, and counters only, so nothing request-derived can pass through.

Sampling never fails a benchmark: an unlocatable cgroup reports and exits zero. The
sampling loop takes an injectable stop predicate so its arithmetic is testable without
delivering a signal.

* rpcbench: collect resource counters during corpus cells

Wires the cgroup sampler around the measured load window only, so node startup and DB
warmup do not dilute the per-request figures, and stages resources.json behind a
numbers-only validator. On by default for corpus runs: the sampler no-ops when the cgroup
cannot be found, and without these counters a cross-client latency gap cannot be
attributed to doing more work, waiting on IO, or leaving cores idle.

* rpcbench: allow one isolation mode for every client

Per-client isolation differed (reth direct, everything else overlay), so cross-client
storage counters compared a harness difference as much as a client one: overlayfs adds a
layer and changes readahead and page-cache behaviour, and disk-read-per-request is the
metric most sensitive to it.

DB_ISOLATION_ALL forces one mode for all clients. Default behaviour is unchanged, since
direct mounts the pristine snapshot read-write and the node's startup writes mutate it -
which is not safe on the Nethermind sets, as expb reuses them. copy gives the same
overlay-free read path while leaving the snapshot intact.

* rpcbench: address the second review round on the corpus mode

- parity-diffs records a word position and direction only. A signed magnitude is
  reversible: with a zero operand the difference IS the other operand, so the artifact
  could publish a complete response word despite the counts-only contract.
- corpus_results dispatches every subcommand explicitly; `comment` fell through to
  `stage` and crashed on a namespace with no output_root.
- Resource sampling moves into run-jsonbench.sh so it brackets container execution
  only, and per-request cost is normalized against the http_reqs count the cell
  actually delivered instead of rate x duration (which assumed an integer-second
  duration and no dropped iterations).
- Sampled figures are cell-local: throttling is a delta and the memory peak is the
  sampled maximum, not the cgroup-lifetime high-water mark that includes warmup.
- Cap overrides parse safely, so a typo such as `250k` degrades to the default
  instead of aborting the sweep at import.
- Adds the sampler suite, zero-operand and cap-parsing regressions, and CLI tests;
  moves unittest.main() below all classes and runs all three suites in CI.

* rpcbench: cover NaN/Infinity rejection in the corpus loader

* rpcbench: give repeated images distinct labels so drift controls survive

* rpcbench: refuse direct isolation on shared snapshots

A direct bind mounts the snapshot read-write, and node startup alone rewrites RocksDB
MANIFEST/CURRENT/WAL and triggers flushes across every column family. The Nethermind
snapshots under /mnt/sda are shared with expb, so one direct run replaces the fixture
every later benchmark compares against.

This is not hypothetical: a direct run on 2026-08-13 mutated
/mnt/sda/nethermind-flat-25490000 (825 changed fingerprint entries) and every later
eth_call corpus measurement showed roughly triple the p99 and a 1.5-2.2% failure rate,
while reth on its own snapshot moved 2%.

`copy` gives the same overlay-free comparison without touching the snapshot, so
DB_ISOLATION_ALL=direct now fails fast unless explicitly acknowledged for a private one.

* rpcbench: warm each node before measuring it

wait_for_rpc gates on eth_blockNumber, which reads the head header and touches no state,
so it returns while the node still cannot serve eth_call. Load then starts against a node
that is up but not serving.

Measured on 2026-08-13 with three identical 100rps cells on one node: cell 1 failed 1.97%
of requests, cell 2 under 1%, cell 3 exactly 0%, and the warm cell reported p99 57ms
against 257ms for the same image measured cold. That 4x tail difference and the ~2%
failures are pure warmup, and every sweep so far ran exactly one cell per node, so this
dominated every comparison the harness has produced.

- Apply CORPUS_WARMUP_DURATION (default 240s, the two cells the evidence required) of
  discarded load per node before its measured cells; set 0 to measure cold on purpose.
- Give a repeated rate its own cell directory. A repeated rate is a drift control, and
  sharing one directory left only the last result behind - which silently reduced the
  three-cell experiment above to a single row.
- Print each cell's failure rate, and warn which percentiles are measuring failures rather
  than latency when it breaches the gate. A 2% failure rate makes p99 a failure statistic,
  which reads as a large regression when nothing became slower.

* rpcbench: record host provenance at the start of a sweep

A reboot or kernel upgrade shifts results persistently and is otherwise invisible in the
logs, so a host change reads as a code regression. On 2026-08-13 a 38% step in one expb
payload set was traced to a machine restart only by noticing that /proc/stat's monotonic
interrupt counter had gone backwards between two runs - the reboot itself was recorded
nowhere.

boot_id identifies a boot directly, and the governor, max frequency, transparent hugepage
mode and CPU mitigation states are the settings most likely to move a benchmark across a
kernel upgrade. Every field degrades to n/a rather than failing, so this cannot break a
sweep on a host that does not expose them.

* rpcbench: apply the corpus record cap in both dispatch modes

The cap is a property of the corpus, not of how the run was dispatched. It was exported
only in the sweep step, so a raised max_corpus_records let the sweep accept a large corpus
while the single-node jsonbench path still rejected the same file at the 10k default.

* rpcbench: source lib.sh in the sweep so provenance logging resolves

run-rpc-sweep.sh never sourced lib.sh, so the log_system_provenance call added with the
provenance logging was an undefined command. Under 'set -uo pipefail' that prints to stderr
and continues, so the sweep still ran and the omission was silent - the first run after the
change recorded no host fingerprint at all. No function names collide between the two files.

* rpcbench: expose corpus_warmup_duration as a dispatch knob

Setting it to 0 measures a cold node on purpose. The cold/warm gap is a result in its own
right - on 2026-08-13 the same binary read p99 91.76 cold and 57.0 warm - so it needs to be
selectable rather than compiled into the default.

(cherry picked from commit 8b48dda1d83ecf7e2d1a4642048038b7287e458c)

* rpcbench: let the single-node path choose the corpus file

The sweep selects a corpus with corpus_glob; the single-node jsonbench path had no
equivalent and always replayed the default file. dotTrace only works on that path
(run-rpc-sweep.sh hardcodes DOTTRACE=false), so a profile could not be taken of the same
corpus the sweeps measure.

(cherry picked from commit 0ffd08d0806b6084f9cea4b07b507d777b43e6f1)

* rpcbench: keep warm-up output out of publication, and warm every measured mode

Four review findings on the warm-up/guard commits:

- The discarded warm-up cell wrote a sanitized summary.json under OUT_DIR as a sibling of
  the rate cells. stage() publishes by filename and comment() keys cells by directory
  position, so 'warmup' and '100' produced the same key and sorted() let the warm-up win -
  the published PR comment would have been built from the cold numbers the warm-up exists
  to discard. Warm-ups now write to scratch, and stage() additionally refuses any path with
  a 'warmup' segment (staging is the boundary, so it enforces this independently).
- Parity/timings-only runs (empty rps_list) got no warm-up at all - the one mode that
  bypasses k6 measured a node proven only to answer eth_blockNumber. Warm-up now runs in
  every mode, at the highest requested cell rate (warming at less leaves faster cells
  partly cold), falling back to the timings rate, then 100 rps. timings.meta.json records
  warmup_seconds so a cold matrix is distinguishable from a warm one after the fact.
- db_isolation_all=direct was documented but unreachable: the guard names an env var no
  dispatcher could set. tool_config now routes db_isolation_allow_snapshot_mutation, and
  the per-client reth default is documented as exempt (its snapshot has no other consumer
  and its post-first-boot state is the fixture every historical reth number used).
- tool_config key lists updated: corpus_file, corpus_warmup_duration, resource_sampling
  (now routable), and the corrected db_isolation_all wording.

* rpcbench: warm the fixture-free mode without the fixture, and make warmup_seconds truthful

Round-three review findings on the warm-up block:

- Warming the timings-only mode through run_cell rebuilt the k6 JSON-array fixture that an
  empty rps_list exists to avoid (GBs on the snapshot volume at large corpus sizes). That
  mode now warms through corpus_parity's paced replay instead - same eth_calls, no k6, no
  fixture - sized as passes = ceil(rate x seconds / records).
- The warm-up cell inherited the 1% fail-rate gate, which rejects exactly the cold-failure
  population the warm-up exists to absorb, inverting its exit status. The gate is lifted
  (JB_MAX_FAIL_RATE_PCT=100) for the warm-up only; report_fail_rate still prints the rate.
- warmup_seconds recorded the request, not the outcome: a failed warm-up still wrote 240,
  and a "4m" duration fell through the seconds parse and wrote 0 ("measured cold") for a
  warm run. The duration is validated up front (integer seconds, optional 's'; "0s"
  disables), and warmup_seconds is derived from the warm-up's actual exit status.
- The staging guard matched a literal 'warmup' segment while the writer produces
  'warmup-cell/'; it now matches any warmup* segment, with the real layout in the test.
- comment() keyed cells by (corpus, label) only, so multi-rate sweeps kept whichever slot
  sorted last and repeated-rate drift controls vanished; cells are keyed by rate slot and
  rendered per slot. cleanup.sh reaps warmup-cell.
- Warm rate now also considers timings_rps when both cells and a matrix are requested.

* rpcbench: bound the replay warm-up by wall clock and record what actually happened

Round-four findings:

- The fixture-free warm-up was bounded by request count, not time: the replay's pacing can
  only delay, so its ceiling is concurrency/latency and a "240s" warm-up on a cold node
  could run ~25 minutes while warmup_seconds recorded 240 - the same states-the-request
  shape fixed on the other axes last round. Both paths now record elapsed wall time, and
  the replay runs under `timeout WARMUP_SECONDS+60`; hitting the bound still counts as
  warmed (the node absorbed load for the whole window), a real crash records 0.
- A missing record count skips the replay warm-up with a warning instead of defaulting to
  1, which timings() would have multiplied by the real count into hours of load.
- The staging guard is anchored to the two positions warm-up output can occupy (scratch
  root, cell slot) so a corpus label containing "warmup" can no longer drop its whole
  scenario from the artifact; regression stages corpus/warmup-heavy/... and asserts it
  survives.
- README documents the warm-up (both paths, cost, duration format) and adds
  warmup_seconds to the matrix-comparability field list.

* rpcbench: record each warm-up path with the clock that is exact for it

Round-five findings:

- Switching the k6 warm-up to an elapsed clock over-corrected: that executor is
  time-bounded, so the requested duration IS the outcome there, and the elapsed delta
  billed the whole json-bench wrapper (clone, docker build, fixture write - which scales
  with corpus size) as warm-up the idle node never received. The k6 branch records the
  request again; the elapsed clock plus timeout stay on the replay branch, whose clock now
  starts at the replay itself.
- The README privacy paragraph enumerated a three-file allowlist while STAGED_FILENAMES
  has eight; it now lists all of them and documents parity-diffs.json - the one artifact
  derived from response bytes - as opt-in and reduced to word positions plus a direction.
  The warm-up is stated as once per corpus per client with the resulting wall-time cost.

* rpcbench: validate and relativize the staged manifest instead of softening the claim

Round-six Low: the README's "each behind an exact-schema validator" was false for
summaries.manifest, which was staged verbatim with runner-absolute paths - the open Low
from round one, now contradicted by the very paragraph that defines the boundary. Rather
than weaken the sentence, the code now honors it: each manifest line is validated against
the iso|/mix| shape, its path is required to resolve inside the output root, and the staged
copy carries artifact-relative paths (the absolute ones exist only for the runner-side
aggregator, which reads the original). jsonbench-summary.md remains the documented single
exception, generated strictly downstream of the sanitized schema.

Also qualifies the warmup_seconds comparability rule: exact-match on k6-warmed runs,
"both warm within a few percent" on replay-warmed runs where the field is measured elapsed.

* rpcbench: manifest pattern matches its consumer's arity; a bad index drops only itself

Round-seven Lows, both on the new _stage_manifest:

- The label class contained '|', so field count was unconstrained while percat-matrix.py
  unpacks exactly 4 fields for iso| and 3 for mix|. The pattern now states each kind's
  arity, so what the README calls validated includes the part a reader assumes: shape AND
  field count.
- A malformed line raised CorpusResultsError out of stage(), and both the artifact upload
  and the PR comment are gated on that step - one bad index line would have discarded every
  validated parity/timings/resources result from a multi-hour sweep, although nothing
  downstream reads the staged manifest at all. The index now drops only itself with a
  ::warning:: while content validators stay fail-closed; regression covers escape,
  shapeless and wrong-arity lines and asserts the content files still stage.

* Use ARM runner for flat benchmarks

* Support ARM benchmark prerequisites

* Bootstrap uv on ARM benchmark runner

* Translate EXPB paths for ARM runner

* Add temporary ARM PR comparison image build

* Use BuildKit for ARM comparison images

* Pass native ARM platform to Docker builder

* Render ARM platform for legacy Docker builder

* Build ARM comparison images with Buildx

* Set up Buildx in ARM image job

* Build rebased ARM comparisons as isolated jobs

* Allow isolated ARM comparison image builds

* rpcbench: pin the sweep to the one configuration the runner can serve

The ARM benchmark runner carries a single snapshot set - Nethermind, flat layout,
under /data/nethermind/nethermind-flat-<block>. The workflow already refuses any
other client or layout, but it reads the top-level inputs that sweep mode
supersedes, so a jsonbench-sweep still defaulted CLIENTS to "nethermind geth
reth": two thirds of the matrix would fail to start (a per-client warning, not an
error) and in corpus mode the baseline would have no candidate to compare
against, so the job would go green with no parity verdict at all.

The sweep now checks both axes before any node starts, and the per-client
snapshot/image/isolation/layout resolution collapses to the single supported
combination. That also retires the reth `direct` isolation default, which was the
one remaining path that mutated a shared snapshot without the consent flag.

Docs follow the data root and the runner label: /mnt/sda -> /data, so the corpus
placement instructions a corpus owner reads name a directory that exists.

Co-authored-by: Kamil Chodoła <43241881+kamilchodola@users.noreply.github.com>

* rpcbench: tighten the supported-configuration wording

* expb: inject client_env into multi-image scenarios too

Multi-image (docker_images) runs silently dropped the client_env input, so A/B
arms needing opt-in env gates (e.g. NETHERMIND_EXPERIMENTAL_SVE2_KECCAK=1) ran
with the feature off. Mirror the single-image injection into the multi-image
render step.

* rpcbench: expose node env vars to sweep runs via tool_config.node_env_vars

start-node.sh already honors NODE_ENV_VARS but no dispatch path could set it;
export it from the sweep step so env-gated experiments benchmark what they claim.

* ci: add ARM runner disk maintenance workflow

The reproducible-benchmarks-arm runner filled its root filesystem (benchmark jobs
failing with 'No space left on device'); this gives us a dispatchable cleanup that
prunes docker debris and runner logs without touching tagged benchmark images.

* ci: install dotnet SDK on the ARM benchmark runner

expb's dotTrace integration fails with 'dotnet CLI not found' on this box;
install the linux-arm64 SDK idempotently so profiling runs work.

* ci: fix dotnet CLI on the ARM runner via DOTNET_ROOT wrapper

A bare symlink into the install dir breaks hostfxr resolution (exit 145);
use a wrapper that sets DOTNET_ROOT, and guard on a working CLI.

* ci: time-bound and self-heal the runner dotnet setup

The unguarded 'dotnet --version' probe wedged the job for its full timeout;
bound every probe, surface the wrapper/muxer state, and rebuild from scratch
when the CLI is broken.

* ci: probe dotnet from a neutral cwd with --list-sdks

The runner's leftover repo checkout pins SDK 10.0.300 in global.json, failing
'dotnet --version' (exit 145) in that cwd even against a healthy install.

* ci: remove stale expb named volumes in runner maintenance

volume prune only touches anonymous volumes; expb's named per-scenario volumes
outlive failed runs and point at deleted output dirs, 500ing later mounts.

* ci: install zip/unzip/file on the ARM runner

The dotTrace archive step dies with 'zip: command not found' on this minimal box.

* ci(arm): stop RPC benchmarks from filling the runner's root disk (#12906)

The ARM box has a ~19G root disk, and filling it kills the docker daemon and the
runner process with it - the runner goes offline until someone restarts it over
SSH. That has now happened three times (2026-08-18, and twice on 2026-08-19),
each time from a dispatch that left docker_image empty: resolve falls through to
image_mode=build and a full Nethermind image is built on a 4-core box with no
room for it. The job dies mid "Prepare Docker image" with no step conclusion and
no logs, which makes it look like an infrastructure blip rather than the input
mistake it is.

Three changes:

- resolve refuses image_mode=build outright and prints how to build the image
  with publish-docker and pass it via docker_image. resolve runs on
  ubuntu-latest, so this fails in seconds without touching the ARM box. It also
  spells out that tool_config `clients` @image entries do not cover this, since
  the top-level image is prepared regardless - the mistake behind all three
  outages.
- the benchmark job reclaims what is safely reclaimable before pulling and
  refuses to start below 6G free, reporting the largest images, rather than
  discovering the shortfall by killing the daemon mid-pull.
- it reclaims again after the run, so pressure cannot accumulate run over run.

Both reclaim steps leave tagged images alone; pinned A/B images must survive
between runs. Clearing that backlog stays a deliberate act via ARM Runner
Maintenance with prune_unused_images=true, which is also noted in that workflow
along with why it carries no cron: schedules only fire from the default branch.

description:
ci: wait for the publish-docker run we dispatched, not any concurrent one (#12907)

* ci: wait for the publish-docker run we dispatched, not any concurrent one

The expb workflow dispatches publish-docker.yml and then waits for it via
wait-for-workflow.sh without telling the script which run to watch, so the script
falls back to discovering one by workflow name + branch. That discovery only
matched `status == "in_progress"`, and a run dispatched seconds earlier is
normally still `queued` - so it skipped the run just requested and latched onto
an older concurrent build of the same branch instead, then reported success.

Observed on run 32278785651: prepare-docker logged

  Run URL: .../actions/runs/32278810049      <- dispatched
  Workflow triggered! Run ID: 32278480843    <- waited on
  The workflow completed successfully!

The job went green while the image it asked for was never pushed, and both
benchmark legs then died pulling a tag that did not exist:

  level=error event="Failed to execute scenario" error="404 ... manifest for
  nethermindeth/nethermind:perf-evm-pool-contention not found"

Two fixes:

- the expb caller now passes RUN_ID from the dispatch action's runId output, so
  it waits on exactly the run it triggered and never races at all.
- the discovery fallback accepts queued runs as well as in_progress ones, and
  sorts numerically, so the other five callers that do not pass a run id stop
  preferring an older run over the one they just triggered.

Also drops `current_time`, which was computed and threaded into the jq call as an
argument the filter never referenced.

* ci: close the remaining discovery race and the silent RUN_ID fallback

Addresses review on #12907.

An empty RUN_ID fell through to discovery instead of failing, which restores the
exact false green this PR removes. benc-uk/workflow-dispatch returns without
setting outputs, and without failing the step, when the target workflow is
disabled, and @v1 is a moving tag that could drop the output - so the wait step
now refuses to continue when runId is empty.

Discovery itself was still racy for the five callers that pass no RUN_ID:
- matching only queued/in_progress still skipped a run in requested, pending or
  waiting (the last whenever the target hits an environment protection rule).
  Inverted to `.status != "completed"`, which covers the whole non-terminal set
  without enumerating statuses that may grow.
- a run is not listed the instant it is dispatched, so on an early poll the
  newest visible entry could still be an unrelated older run, and the loop would
  break on it. Restored a created_at floor - the variable the previous commit
  deleted was computed for this and never wired into the filter - so an older run
  cannot match and the loop keeps polling until the intended run appears.

Verified against synthetic API payloads: a fresh `requested` run now wins over an
older `in_progress` one (2, previously 1); a lone older run matches nothing so
polling continues; `waiting` is matched; `completed` and other branches are not.

description:
feat(xdc): read XDPoS rewards as XDC amounts (#12852)

* feat(xdc): read XDPoS rewards as XDC amounts

The reference client states masternode, protector and observer rewards in
XDC and scales them to wei on load, so Apothem's genesis carries values
such as 63420000000000001704 rather than a round 6.342e19. Nethermind's
chainspec copied those pre-converted integers, which left the client
unable to read a reference genesis and left the odd constants
unexplained.

Add a converter that reproduces the reference conversion exactly: decode
the literal to a float64, form the exact product with 10^18, round it to
a 64-bit significand and truncate toward zero. Neither double nor decimal
arithmetic reaches those values, so the product is built in BigInteger
and rounded explicitly.

Apply it per property, which confines the unit convention to
engine.XDPoS.params: the converters registered on EthereumJsonSerializer
are untouched, so the rest of the chainspec and JSON-RPC keep rejecting
fractional numbers as EIP-1474 requires. Restate the Apothem rewards as
the reference amounts; a test loads the shipped file and pins the wei
they resolve to.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* fix(xdc): keep networkInformation serializable, guard the wei migration

V2ConfigParams is not only a chainspec type: it is the XDPoS_networkInformation
response DTO, reached through XDPoSConfig.V2Configs. A property-level
JsonConverter applies on write, so the NotSupportedException thrown by
XdcToWeiConverter.Write landed mid-object once the response had begun
serializing. Write now emits wei, exactly what the endpoint produced before,
and a test serializes the response to pin it.

Reading XDC while writing wei is asymmetric, but deliberate: operators
configure in XDC as the reference does, and the API reports wei as every other
Ethereum endpoint does. Nothing round-trips the type.

Bound the amount at 10^12 XDC. UInt256 overflow was the only ceiling, and a
reward left in the previous wei spelling is ~10^18 times any real value yet
still far inside UInt256 -- so it started the node and inflated every payout
silently. Above the bound the load now fails with a message naming the unit.

Also correct the two README entries still documenting these fields as Wei,
reject negative zero, defer the literal to the throw paths, and select the
Apothem config by switch round rather than position.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 

* revert(xdc): drop the reward plausibility bound

No subnets have been deployed, and the shipped chainspecs are embedded in
the build and replaced on upgrade, so there is no wei-denominated config
for the bound to catch. It was guarding a migration that cannot happen.

Restore the UInt256 overflow check the bound had made unreachable, which
also makes the "beyond UInt256 once scaled" case exercise what its name
claims again. Assert all three rewards in the networkInformation test
rather than the masternode one alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5

description:
Add error-category telemetry to SshTunnelEvent (#6321)

## Changes

Add `error_category` to `SshTunnelEvent`
(`libs/telemetry/protos/ssh_tunnel.go`) and set it at each failure site
in the `ssh connect` flow
(`experimental/ssh/internal/client/client.go`). Categories name the
distinct early-return sites — `IDE_COMMAND_NOT_ON_PATH`,
`CLUSTER_ACCESS_DENIED`, `SERVER_START_TIMEOUT`, `USER_ABORTED`, etc. —
so no raw error text, cluster name, or path is logged.

Two details worth a reviewer's attention:

- The telemetry `defer` now registers before the IDE precondition
checks. It sat *after* them, so `--ide` failures on a missing
`code`/`cursor` command returned early and emitted **no event at all**.
They were not merely uncategorized, they were absent from the failure
counts entirely.
- The field is declared without `omitempty`, so a success sends
`TYPE_UNSPECIFIED` explicitly rather than collapsing to a null that
cannot be told apart from a CLI too old to report the field.

The failure outcome is collected in a small `connectOutcome` struct and
`Run` uses a named return, so the deferred logger observes the error the
caller sees. A cancelled context maps to `USER_ABORTED` and takes
precedence over the category recorded at the failure site, since Ctrl-C
surfaces as a cancellation from whichever call happens to observe it
first.

## Why

IDE-mode connections have a 40–55% failure rate, but telemetry only
records *that* a connection failed, so the cause is invisible. The
leading hypothesis was that `CheckIDECommand` rejects users whose IDE
shell command is not on PATH — a permanent per-machine condition, which
matches the observed stickiness (a retry after a failed first attempt
succeeds only 17–21% of the time).

That hypothesis was untestable for a second reason beyond the missing
field: those checks ran before the telemetry defer, so they produced no
event. Adding the field alone would not have confirmed or refuted it.
This also means the sub-5s failure bucket in the original analysis could
not have contained the PATH failures.

Deliberately left uncategorized: the malformed `--metadata` paths fall
through to `UNKNOWN`. `--metadata` is a hidden flag whose value the CLI
generates itself in `ToProxyCommand`, so a parse failure is a CLI bug,
not a user-environment blocker. Mapping it to `SERVER_START_TIMEOUT`
would pollute the bucket that tracks unreachable servers.

Scope note: `is_success` still carries `omitempty`, so failures remain
NULL rather than `false`. That is tracked separately and not touched
here. Until it changes, count failures via `error_category` (`NOT IN
('TYPE_UNSPECIFIED')`, plus an `IS NOT NULL` guard for rows from CLIs
predating this field) rather than `is_success = false`.

The matching backend schema change has landed, so these values are
queryable once this rolls out. Every enum spelling matches the constants
added here exactly: the CLI serializes the enum name as a string, so a
drift would silently decode to `TYPE_UNSPECIFIED` rather than fail
loudly.

## Tests

Unit tests in `client_internal_test.go` cover the category mapping:
success reports `TYPE_UNSPECIFIED`, an attributed failure keeps its
category, an unattributed one falls back to `UNKNOWN`, a cancellation
reports `USER_ABORTED` and wins over the site category, and a non-zero
exit *after* the tunnel is up is not counted as a connection failure.

Verified locally: `./task test-exp-ssh` (278 unit + 4 acceptance) and
full `./task lint` (0 issues, all three modules).

I also drove `Run` with `PATH` emptied — the exact condition of the
hypothesis above, since `CheckIDECommand` resolves the IDE command with
`exec.LookPath`. The emitted payload is:

```json
{"compute_type":"DEDICATED","ide_type":"vscode","client_mode":"IDE",
 "server_start_time_ms":0,"error_category":"IDE_COMMAND_NOT_ON_PATH"}
```

That confirms an event is emitted at all on this path, and that every
category serializes to one of the declared enum names.

Still not verified end to end against real compute — no event has been
observed landing in the telemetry table. Worth doing before this is
relied on for dashboards.

No changelog fragment: the feature is under `experimental/` and this is
internal telemetry, matching #4881 and #6058.

_This PR was written by Claude Code._

direct: add DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_RESOURCE_MAX_WAIT to cap resource waits (#6263)

## Changes

`DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_RESOURCE_MAX_WAIT` (in seconds) caps how long deploy
and destroy wait for a resource to reach its target state. On expiry the
wait is abandoned with a warning rather than failing the deploy: state
is saved before the wait, so the resource stays tracked and the next
deploy reconciles it. `0` skips the wait without issuing a request.

A resource keeps its full wait when something that runs after it needs
it provisioned. Its own `.permissions` / `.grants` children do not
count: they reference nothing but the parent's id, which `DoCreate`
returns before the wait starts. Deletes are capped regardless of
dependents, except the delete inside recreate, which has to release the
name for the create that follows. Direct engine only.

Applied to the vector search index tests that only need the index to
exist, not to be queryable: `basic`, `grants/select`, and the
`vector_search_index` invariant configs. All three now run on every PR
rather than nightly-only, and the invariants are no longer excluded from
cloud at all.

## Why

Vector Search index provisioning takes 15-30 minutes, which made these
by far the slowest tests on cloud.

env with the cap removed and `TimeoutCloud` raised to 90m. That last
part matters: two of the six variants took over 25m uncapped, which is
the default `TimeoutCloud`, so enabling them without the cap would time
out rather than merely be slow. After is run 32253634089 on this PR. The
`invariants` range spans six variants per env: `no_drift`,
`delete_idempotent` and `destroy_idempotent`, each with and without
`READPLAN`.

## What stays slow

`recreate/embedding_dimension` (13-21m) keeps its full waits and stays
`CloudSlow`. Capping it breaks the test: the capped create leaves the
index provisioning, so the recreate then deletes a provisioning index
and exceeds the 15m `deleteIndexTimeout`. Capping the recreate's delete
wait too would just move the failure to `pendingDeletionTimeout`.

The cap is set per config rather than for the whole invariant directory
on purpose. This index is three orders of magnitude slower than the next
slowest invariant config (`cluster`, ~100s), and capping every config
would leave nothing exercising a real `WaitAfterCreate` against a real
backend.

## Tests

Unit tests for parsing, the child-dependency rule and the wait
semantics, including that a genuine failure still fails the deploy and
that cancelling the deployment is not swallowed. Two acceptance tests:
`resource-max-wait` covers parsing, and `resource-max-wait-zero` covers
what the cap does to a wait — it deploys a cluster with the cap at 0 and
asserts the poll GET is absent, since the test server only advances a
cluster from PENDING to RUNNING on read, so the missing poll is what
proves the resource was left unwaited.

Cloud-checked rather than assumed: a capped create does not produce
spurious drift. `grants/select` re-plans to `0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to
delete` and `no_drift` passes `verify_no_drift.py` (which requires every
action to be `skip`) on all six clouds. The grant also applies to an
index that is not ready yet, and the two idempotency invariants survive
deleting an index whose first delete was cut short.

description:
apps: stop planning an update on every deploy (#6328)

## Changes

The direct engine planned an Apps update on every deploy, so each
`bundle deploy` issued a no-op `Apps.CreateUpdate` call. Every plan
looked like this, with a remote value and no local one:

```json
"forward_user_access_token": { "action": "update", "remote": true }
```

`forward_user_access_token` became part of `apps.App` in
databricks-sdk-go v0.171.0 (#6320) and was added to the app update mask,
but nothing classified it. The backend enables token forwarding and
reports it as `true` even when the bundle omits the field, so the remote
`true` read as drift, `hasAppChanges` returned true, and the update
fired.

Declared under `backend_defaults`, exactly like `compute_size`: the
remote value is skipped when the config omits the field, while an
explicit value in the config still diffs normally (so real drift is
still caught).

Migrate bundle state filer read off workspace-files to /workspace/export (#6219)

# bundle: read deploy state via /workspace/export instead of deprecated
workspace-files API

## Summary

Switch the DABs state filer read (`bundle/deploy/filer.go`,
`stateFiler.Read`) from
`GET /api/2.0/workspace-files/{path}` to the SDK's
`Workspace.Download(ctx, absPath)`, which issues
`GET /api/2.0/workspace/export?path=&direct_download=true`. This
reads the bundle state files
(`terraform.tfstate`, `resources.json`) from the workspace.

## Why

The `workspace-files` endpoint is deprecated and is mapped to **no API
scope**. Under context-based
ingress (CBI) with fine-grained scoped tokens it was only reachable via
the `all_apis` master scope,
so `bundle deploy` returned 403s for customers on least-privilege scoped
tokens. `/workspace/export`
is properly scoped, so state reads now work under least-privilege auth.

## Implementation

Reads go through the SDK's `Workspace.Download` helper, so there is no
separate API client, no manual
`auth.WorkspaceIDHeaders` routing headers (the SDK sets these), and no
intermediate buffer —
`Download` returns the streaming body directly.

`direct_download=true` is load-bearing: plain `/workspace/export`
returns base64 JSON capped at 10 MB,
while the streaming variant handles files up to 500 MB, so large state
files stream through fine.

## Testing

- Regenerated acceptance goldens: request traces now show `GET
/api/2.0/workspace/export` with
  `direct_download=true` (`user_agent`, `state` suites).
- Validated against a real workspace (dogfood): streaming export returns
the state bytes correctly
  end-to-end.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

Cover reading .git with an acceptance test and drop the git-metadata integration tests (#6316)

Follow-up to https://github.com/databricks/cli/pull/6303.

## Why
Every case in `integration/libs/git/git_fetch_test.go` is now covered by
an
acceptance test, which runs locally against the fake server as well as
against a
real workspace, rather than only against a workspace.

Most of it was already covered:

- The API cases by `acceptance/bundle/debug/fetch-repository-info`,
which asserts the
same four fields for a Git folder root and a subdirectory, and also for
a folder
  outside `/Repos` and a path in no Git folder, on every cloud.
- A path outside a repository by every acceptance test that runs outside
one, where
  `bundle.git` is just `{"bundle_root_path": "."}`.
- An unreadable `.git` by `acceptance/bundle/git-permerror`.

Two things were not, so this adds `acceptance/bundle/git-metadata` for
them:

- No acceptance test read an **origin URL or commit** from `.git`.
`git-repo-init`
creates no remote, and `bundle/variables/git-branch` deletes
`bundle.git.commit`
as non-deterministic, so an empty commit was indistinguishable from a
real one.
- A **malformed** `.git` was only covered by `git-permerror`, which
needs `chmod`
  and so carries `GOOS.windows = false`.

`TestFetchRepositoryInfoAPI_FromRepo` was also the only test in the
package that
creates a Git folder, and cloning bundle-examples on GCP takes around
64s against
the SDK's 60s client timeout, so it failed there before reaching an
assertion:

```
Creating repo: /Repos/.../integration-test-...
Error: Post ".../api/2.0/repos": request timed out after 1m0s of inactivity
--- FAIL: TestFetchRepositoryInfoAPI_FromRepo (60.68s)
```

Its `known_failures.txt` entry, left from the metadata bug fixed in
#6303, hid that
from the Integration Tests result.

## Changes
`acceptance/bundle/git-metadata` covers a repository with an `origin`
remote,
asserting branch, commit and origin URL come from `.git`, and a `.git`
file with no
`gitdir` line, asserting the worktree root is still found with no
metadata. It runs
on every platform.

The malformed case keeps validate's report out of the golden: the
message names the
`.git` path, and `worktree.go` builds it with `filepath.Join`, so its
separators
differ per platform. `musterr` asserts the command fails and
`contains.py` asserts
the report, so neither depends on how the path is spelled.

`git_fetch_test.go` is deleted. `TestGitClone*` stay, in
`git_clone_test.go`.

## Tests
`integration/libs/git` passes on aws, azure and gcp with the default
timeout, where
gcp needed a raised one before. The package now runs in ~3.5s rather
than 28-76s.

The full acceptance suite passes, and `bundle/git-metadata` was checked
to fail when
the `contains.py` needle is wrong, so the assertion is live.

description:
Read git metadata from the Repos API for Git CLI folders (#6303)

## Why
A Git folder that has Git CLI access is a workspace DIRECTORY whose git
metadata is
not stored on the workspace object, so
`workspace/get-status?return_git_info=true`
returns only `id` and `path` for it - no `branch`, `head_commit_id` or
`url`. Those
fields are declared unconditionally in the API, and
`fetchRepositoryInfoAPI` copied
them straight into `RepositoryInfo`, so on DBR `bundle.git.branch`,
`.commit` and
`.origin_url` silently became empty.

New Git folders are created this way as the `wsfs_git_cli` public
preview ramps up
(SDR-3545), which is what broke `TestFetchRepositoryInfoAPI_FromRepo` on
all clouds.
It is not a propagation race: polling get-status for 90s never fills the
fields in,
so there is nothing to retry.

## Changes
When get-status returns a git folder id but no metadata, read it from
`Repos.Get`.
`git_info.id` is the id of the Git folder root even when the queried
path is a
subdirectory, so both the root and subdir cases resolve. A legacy REPO
folder still
answers from get-status alone and makes no extra call.

This also reverts the GCP skip from
https://github.com/databricks/cli/pull/6038 -
that skip described this same gap, which reached GCP first.

## Tests
New unit tests for `fetchRepositoryInfoAPI` covering full metadata
(asserting no
Repos call), the fallback, a subdirectory, a failing `Repos.Get`, and a
path with no
git info. `integration/libs/git` passes against aws, azure and gcp.

description:
localenv: keep every pre-run pyproject.toml via timestamped backups (#6268)

## Changes

`environments setup-local` rewrites the managed regions of a project's
`pyproject.toml` on each run. Previously it backed the file up to
`pyproject.toml.bak` **once** (the pristine pre-first-sync original) and
never refreshed it. So if a user edited a managed region between syncs —
`requires-python`, the `databricks-connect` pin, `[tool.uv]`, or
`[tool.databricks.environment]` — the next run overwrote that edit and
no backup captured it: `.bak` still held the older original, leaving the
pre-run state unrecoverable.

This change makes the backup capture **every** pre-run state:

- Before any run that will actually change `pyproject.toml`, the current
file is backed up. The first backup keeps the canonical
`pyproject.toml.bak` name (the permanent pristine original); once that
exists, each later modifying run writes a distinct
`pyproject.toml..bak` (local-time stamp), with a `-N` suffix
on a same-second collision — so no prior state is ever clobbered.
- A no-op re-run (merged output already on disk) writes no backup, so an
idempotent re-sync neither rewrites `pyproject.toml` nor clutters the
directory.
- Backups are written with `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` (`writeNew`): creation is
atomic and fails rather than overwriting, so a write can never destroy
an earlier backup and two runs can't both claim one name. A partially
written file (e.g. `ENOSPC` mid-write) is removed so it can't masquerade
as a complete backup or block a later run from reclaiming the canonical
name. The source file's permission bits are preserved onto the backup.
- `--dry-run` `wouldBackup` mirrors the real run: reported only when the
run would change the file, named `.bak` or timestamped as the real run
would name it.

## Tests

- A modifying re-run writes a timestamped backup of the current content
while keeping `.bak` as the original; a no-op re-run writes no new
backup; same-second backups get unique names; `writeNew` refuses to
overwrite and preserves mode; first-run `--dry-run` plans the canonical
`.bak`.
- `go test ./libs/localenv/` (197) and `./cmd/environments/` (29) pass;
`go vet` and `gofmt` clean.

This pull request and its description were written by Isaac.

Render the DCM changeset tree with Rich's `Tree` component (#201)

The changeset tree was drawn by hand: four guide-glyph constants plus a
recursive `_render_nodes` that threaded an indentation prefix down the
recursion and wrote each row as a burst of up to eleven
`cli_console.styled_message()` calls, each one a separate render and write.
`rich.tree.Tree` already does this, and the same plugin used it for the
upload-files tree, so the hand-rolled renderer was redundant.

Each `_ChangeNode` now returns a `rich.text.Text` label instead of emitting
to the console, and `Tree` owns the layout. `CompactTree` keeps DCM's
three-column guides (`├─ `) rather than Rich's four (`├── `) by overriding
the two guide attributes `Tree` documents for that purpose, so the changeset
tree renders byte-for-byte as before — verified against a synthetic changeset
covering every node kind, six nesting levels, the `removed` collapse, entity
ordering and the blank-line separators. The upload-files tree shares
`CompactTree` too, so both DCM trees now draw the same guides.

`cli_console.renderable()` prints with soft wrap off. The global Rich console
sets `soft_wrap = True` so a URL in a plain message survives wrapping, but
under soft wrap Rich crops every row of a renderable at the console width —
silently, with no ellipsis. That would have swallowed the right-hand side of
any change line wider than the terminal, discarding the work
`_truncate_value_pair` does to keep the changed segment visible. Long rows now
wrap with the continuation indented under the change. It also means the upload
tree's `overflow="ellipsis"` takes effect for the first time.

Report dbt fmt fixes as LSP diagnostics, gated by lsp.formatter.enabled

* Report dbt fmt fixes as LSP diagnostics, gated by lsp.formatter.enabled

The LSP cannot mutate a user's source files, so instead of applying dbt fmt's
fixes it now computes what would change and reports each edit as an
informational diagnostic (data.replacement + data.category), letting
downstream consumers (e.g. dbt Cloud's LSP client) apply the fix themselves.
Off by default; opt in via the new lsp.formatter.enabled client-config setting,
independent of the existing lint toggle.

Also fixes a related inconsistency: the diagnostics pass always used the
Rendered jinja-render algorithm regardless of the project's configured
jinja_render_mode, and .sqlfluff (including that setting) was only loaded when
the linter toggle was enabled, even though the formatter toggle can be enabled
on its own. Both the linter and the new formatter-diagnostics pass now branch
on jinja_render_mode consistently with dbt fmt/dbt lint, and .sqlfluff loads
whenever either feature is on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 

* Support jinja_render_mode = symbolic for dbt fmt/lint --fix and LSP formatter-diagnostics

Symbolic mode's taint-aware rendering (added in #12848) only covered linting;
formatting/fixing under `--jinja-render-mode symbolic` was rejected outright
because reconciling fixes across multiple tainted-branch variants back onto
one source file was an open question. It turns out format already had the
machinery to do exactly that merge (`merge_source_patches`/
`suppress_conditional_block_indent_trims`, built for sqlfluff's own heuristic
reflow-variant guessing) -- it just never got real branch-variant input.

Adds `render_symbolic_format_targets`, the format-pipeline counterpart of
`render_symbolic_lint_targets`: it renders each tainted `{% if %}` decision's
alternate branch (mirroring the lint-side exploration) and builds a
`TemplatedFile` per variant by combining `SymbolicRenderingEventListener`
(taint/branch-override) with `SqlfluffTemplatedFileListener` (position
tracking for reflow) in one render pass, sharing one output-tracker location
the same way `DefaultRenderingEventListenerFactory` already does elsewhere.
Required a small new `SymbolicRenderingEventListener::with_tracker`
constructor mirroring the existing `DefaultRenderingEventListener` one.

`compute_format_result` now feeds every variant `render_format_target_for_path`
returns into its existing merge loop (skipping the sqlfluff heuristic-variant
step when real branch data is already available), so both the CLI's

description:
fix(cli): keep the requested folder when downloading a single file (#1181)

## Summary

`kaggle datasets download -f ` and `kaggle competitions download
-f ` named the output file from the last segment of the signed
storage URL and ignored the requested path, so a file inside a folder
was written to the destination root. Two files sharing a base name
resolved to the same local path, and one request would leave the other
file's contents on disk while exiting 0.

## Problem

`jpmiller/publicassistance` is public and about 300 KB. It has four
folders that each contain a `Food_Costs.csv`.

```bash
kaggle datasets download jpmiller/publicassistance -f WICAgencies2013ytd/Food_Costs.csv -p out
kaggle datasets download jpmiller/publicassistance -f WICAgencies2014ytd/Food_Costs.csv -p out
```

Before this change, both commands wrote to `out/Food_Costs.csv`. The
second request was skipped because a file of that name already existed,
so it exited 0 and left the 2013 file in place:

```text
WICAgencies2013ytd/Food_Costs.csv   12695 bytes   sha256 9933552f3403d281...
WICAgencies2014ytd/Food_Costs.csv   12681 bytes   sha256 3cd6049ae8de4336...
out/Food_Costs.csv                  12695 bytes   sha256 9933552f3403d281...
```

Downloading the whole dataset with `--unzip` reproduces the folders, and
`kernels output` already writes to `os.path.join(target_dir,
item.file_name)`. Only the single file download path flattened.

## Solution

`_resolve_download_path()` takes the directory from the requested
`file_name` and the base name from the download URL, then checks the
result with the existing `_is_within_directory()`.

The base name has to keep coming from the URL because large files are
served compressed. `creditcard.csv` arrives as `creditcard.csv.zip`, and
only the URL records that. Using the whole requested path would write a
zip archive named `.csv`.

A `file_name` with no directory part resolves exactly as before, so flat
downloads and the compressed base name behavior are unchanged.

Both call sites now resolve through the same helper. `download_file()`
already creates the parent directory, so nothing else was needed there.

After this change:

```text
out/WICAgencies2013ytd/Food_Costs.csv   12695 bytes   sha256 9933552f3403d281...
out/WICAgencies2014ytd/Food_Costs.csv   12681 bytes   sha256 3cd6049ae8de4336...
```

## Behavior change

A nested `-f` download now lands under the requested folder instead of
the destination root. This is a change for anyone relying on the file
arriving at the root. I have made it unconditional rather than gating it
behind a flag, since the current placement can leave a different file
than the one requested, but I am happy to gate it if you would rather
keep the existing layout as the default.

## Testing

- [x] `hatch -e test run pytest tests/unit/test_download_file_paths.py
-v` (17 passed)
- [x] `hatch -e test run pytest tests/unit` (1303 passed, 3 skipped)
- [x] `hatch run lint:all`
- [x] Verified against the live API: the two `Food_Costs.csv` files now
land side by side with the hashes above, `creditcard.csv` still arrives
as `creditcard.csv.zip`, a flat file is unchanged, and `competitions
download -f kaggle_evaluation/core/__init__.py` writes the nested path
- [ ] Maintainer: please run `/gcbrun` when convenient

New tests cover a flat path, a nested path, deep nesting, two files
sharing a base name, a compressed response with and without a folder,
backslash separators, dot and repeated separators, a leading separator,
and three traversal inputs. The three behavior tests fail against the
previous code.

Docs updated in `docs/datasets.md`, `docs/competitions.md`,
`skills/references/datasets.md`, and
`skills/references/competitions.md`.

## Related

Fixes #1178
